So, this is probably going to be a long story but I'm so angry I think my head is going to literally explode, and I need an outlet. Apologies in advance for length.

My friend: ER nurse in a busy, 45ish bed trauma center ER.

Ham planet patient: Late 20s, literal incarnation of the textbook tumblerina, complete with greasy rainbow neon hair, massive fupa, SJW-approved T-shirt, and in this particular case complete with a home oxygen tank and bariatric sized wheelchair. Her (its?) chief complaint was chest pain and shortness of breath, cough and fever.

The story, in my friends words, with some editing of medical jargon for the uninitiated by me:

Pt and entourage roll up via POV to the ambulance bay. Pt's mother (equally grotesque planetary status ham) gets out and pounds on the glass doors to the ambulance bay. Myself and an EMT go out to see what's up. Pt precedes to whine that she needs a wheelchair and can't possibly walk inside. How she managed to get her substantial self into the car in the first place is a subject I didn't broach. Regardless, she said the magical "chest pain" words which granted her an immediate ride to a room, EKG and blood work to rule out an MI. Unfortunately the room she got a ride to was my trauma bay thanks to bed availability.

So the EKG is negative, and blood work is cooking. I proceed to triage, assess and interview the patient. Get through the extensive history, including weight loss surgery, PCOS, hypothyroidism, CHF, arthritis, etc. The pt is labored and wheezing so hard from the exertion of going from a laying to sitting position in bed the idea of having to intubate crosses my mind, having already listened to her massively abnormal breath sounds. My next question is her height and weight, because should we have to breath for her I'll need the info to tell the doc how deep to place the tube and to calculate medication doses. This is a standard question that gets asked of every patient that comes through triage, the fact that she got a ticket straight back to a bed didn't change the fact that I legitimately needed the info. Heck, people tell me "I don't know how much I weigh" all the time, and it's not a big deal. I'm good at guessing, it's just always better to get it straight from the patient if getting them on a scale isn't immediately possible. Which it wasn't.

Let me just stop here and say that my treatment of the patient throughout our entire encounter was 100% cool, calm and professional. I'm not a new nurse. I have a damn good game face.

So, I ask the pt, "do you know your height and weight?" In my sweet, nonjudgmental tone (my friend really does come off as sweet, nonjudgmental and easy to talk to, she's trained to interview kids who may have been sexuality assaulted). Pt says "uh, I don't really know." I say "it's ok, no big deal" and prepare to move on to my next line of questioning. Before I could get the next sentence out though, pt interrupts me and says "I'm 5'6" and about 160lbs". I keep my professional cool, laughing on the inside because there's no way that someone that big who is easily 5" shorter than me only weighs 30 lbs more than myself. I quickly click back to the right screen to chart her stated height and weight, and politely repeat the numbers back to her to verify them. I then move on with my interview.

The rest of her ER course was uneventful, cardiac workup was negative and she was discharged home with a respiratory ailment, chronic conditions and a new prescription.

She departed the department around 11am. Around 1pm, I'm called into the charge office. Apparently the patient called to complain to the nurse manager that I "humiliated and degraded" her by asking her weight not once but twice, and she was subsequently unable to participate in her own care due to the mental anguish it caused. Additionally, she claimed that her pain was never addressed and she was in excruciating 10/10 pain the entire time she was in the ER, despite the fact that I medicated her repeatedly for pain, albeit at a dose appropriate for a 160lb pt. The director sided with the patient and wrote me up, even though my actions were 100% by policy. Policy is to obtain height and weight on every ER patient, and to verify all information provided by the patient at the time it's entered into the EMR. Yet I still get a write up. I refused to sign it, and I'm suspended for 3 days pending an investigation. I have no doubt my doc will back my care as appropriate, so my only hope is that the disciplinary panel will interview him or accept the letter he says he will write regarding the situation on my behalf.

She went on to describe how emotionally distraught the whole situation has made her. She is a very good nurse, and never had any sort of disciplinary actions in the past.

I'm beyond angry for her. In what world does this actually happen? How is this ok? I'm livid, I've never in my life wanted to physically hurt someone but I'm bordering on it now thanks to what this "person" is putting my friend through.
